title: Review: Thermal energy transfers
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: B.1#c30 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c32 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c20 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c02 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: B.1#q15, B.1#q34, B.1#q19, B.1#q36, B.1#q22, B.1#q37, B.1#q25, B.1#q27, B.1#q29, B.1#q28. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Convection
items.clue: Transfer of thermal energy in a fluid (liquid or gas) by bulk movement of the fluid itself.

items.label: Thermal radiation
items.clue: Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves emitted from the surface of a body because of its temperature.

items.label: Evaporation
items.clue: The change from liquid to gas that takes place only at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature, not only at the boiling point.

items.label: Solid (molecular model)
items.clue: Particles are closely packed, held by strong intermolecular forces in fixed mean positions, often in a regular arrangement, and vibrate about those positions.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium and a 0.50 kg block of copper, both at 20 °C, are each supplied with 9.0 kJ of energy. Specific heat capacities: aluminium 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, copper 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume no energy is lost. Which statement about their final temperatures is correct?

options.text: The aluminium ends at about 66 °C, the copper at 40 °C.
They end at the same temperature, as each gets 9.0 kJ.
The copper ends at about 66 °C and the aluminium at 40 °C.
The copper ends at about 46 °C and the aluminium at only 20 °C.

questions.explanation: ΔT = Q/(mc). Aluminium: 9000/(0.50 × 900) = 20 K, so 20 + 20 = 40 °C. Copper: 9000/(0.50 × 390) = 46 K, so 20 + 46 = 66 °C. The smaller c gives the larger rise.

questions.stem: On a still evening a person stands 2 m to one side of a bonfire, at the same height as the flames, and feels warmth on their face. By which mechanism does most of this energy reach their face, and why?

options.text: Conduction: the hot air next to the flames passes energy from particle to particle across the 2 m of still air to the person's face.
Convection: heat is a fluid that spreads out from the fire through the air in every direction, including sideways to the face.
Radiation: still air is a poor conductor, and the hot air from the fire rises, so neither conduction nor convection carries much energy sideways.
Convection: the heat from the fire rises, and as it spreads it warms the whole of the surrounding air, including the air by the person's face.

questions.stem: The rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction is given by ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx). What does the minus sign show?

options.text: The rate of energy transfer falls steadily with time and along the length of the conductor.
Cold is conducted in the opposite direction to heat, from the cold end to the hot end.
Energy flows towards lower temperature: where T falls along +x, the net flow is along +x.
The conductor is losing energy, so ΔQ/Δt is a negative quantity for every conducting material.

questions.explanation: Where the temperature decreases along +x, ΔT/Δx is negative, so −kA(ΔT/Δx) is positive: energy flows in the +x direction, from hot to cold. The minus sign encodes the direction of flow.

questions.stem: In a simple refrigerator the freezing compartment is placed at the top of the cabinet. Which statement explains why this cools the whole of the space below it?

options.text: Heat naturally rises, so the thermal energy from all the food travels upwards to the compartment at the top, where it is removed from the cabinet.
Coldness is a heavy substance that is produced by the compartment and pours down through the cabinet, filling it from the bottom upwards like water.
Air cooled by the compartment becomes denser and sinks, and the warmer air below rises to replace it, so a convection current circulates.
The air molecules next to the compartment shrink and become heavier as they cool, so each one falls to the bottom of the cabinet under its own weight.

questions.stem: Star X has 1.2 times the radius of star Y and 1.5 times its surface temperature (in kelvin). Both stars are modelled as black bodies. What is the ratio (luminosity of X)/(luminosity of Y)?
Star A has 100 times the luminosity of star B, yet from the Earth star A appears dimmer than star B. Which statement must be correct?

options.text: We receive more power per unit area from A than from B.
At equal distances, A and B would look equally bright.
B must have a much hotter surface than A has.
A lies much further from the Earth than B does.

questions.explanation: Apparent brightness is the power received per unit area at the observer, and it depends on both the star's luminosity and its distance. A star that emits 100 times as much power can only appear dimmer if its light is spread over a much larger sphere, so it must be much further away.

questions.stem: Star P has a luminosity of 16 L⊙ and is at a distance 4d from the Earth. Star Q has a luminosity of 1 L⊙ and is at a distance d. How does the apparent brightness of P compare with that of Q?

options.text: They appear equally bright: 16 times the luminosity offsets 4 times the distance.
P appears 16 times as bright as Q, because it is 16 times as luminous.
P appears 4 times as bright as Q, as brightness is proportional to 1/d.
Q appears the brighter of the two, because Q is nearer to the Earth.

questions.explanation: b = L/4πd². b_P/b_Q = (L_P/L_Q) × (d_Q/d_P)² = 16 × (1/4)² = 16/16 = 1. P's sixteen-fold luminosity exactly compensates for its four-fold distance.

questions.stem: The black-body spectrum of star X peaks at 290 nm and that of star Y peaks at 870 nm. The two stars have the same radius. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Y has three times the surface temperature of X and has 81 times the luminosity.
X has three times the surface temperature of Y and three times the luminosity.
X has three times the surface temperature of Y, and 81 times its luminosity.
X and Y may be equally hot; the peak shows only what each star is made of.

questions.explanation: λ_max T = constant, so T_X/T_Y = 870/290 = 3. With equal radii, L ∝ T⁴, so L_X/L_Y = 3⁴ = 81.

questions.stem: Water in an electric kettle is boiling at 100 °C. The 2.0 kW heater stays switched on for a further 2.5 minutes. Assume all the energy supplied is transferred to the water. Specific latent heat of vaporization of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What mass of water boils away?
A black body is heated to a higher temperature. How does its emission spectrum change?

options.text: It emits more at every wavelength, and the peak moves to a longer wavelength.
It emits more at every wavelength, and its peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
Its peak moves to shorter wavelengths, so it emits less at long wavelengths.
It emits only one wavelength, λ_max, which gets shorter as it gets hotter.

questions.explanation: A hotter black body emits more intensely at every wavelength, so the whole curve rises, and by Wien's law λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T the peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
